questions.stem: Which of the following fractions is the GREATEST in value: 3/7, 4/9, 5/11, or 6/13?

options.option_text: The greatest fraction among the four is 3/7
The greatest fraction among the four is 4/9
The greatest fraction among the four is 5/11
The greatest fraction among the four is 6/13

questions.explanation: D is correct. Converting to decimals: 3/7 ≈ 0.4286, 4/9 ≈ 0.4444, 5/11 ≈ 0.4545, 6/13 ≈ 0.4615. So 6/13 is the greatest. A common error is choosing 5/11, because 5 appears 'close to half of 11', but 6/13 is slightly larger. **Short Trick:** All four fractions are of the form n/(2n+1) with n = 3, 4, 5, 6. The function n/(2n+1) is strictly increasing — a larger n always gives a larger value. Pick the one with the largest n, i.e., 6/13.

questions.stem: A man spent 2/5 of his monthly salary on food and 1/4 of the remaining amount on rent. If he saved ₹5,400 at the end of the month, what was his monthly salary?

options.option_text: The monthly salary of the man comes to ₹10,000
The monthly salary of the man comes to ₹12,000
The monthly salary of the man comes to ₹15,000
The monthly salary of the man comes to ₹13,500

questions.explanation: B is correct. Let salary = x. Food = 2x/5, so remaining = 3x/5. Rent = (1/4) × (3x/5) = 3x/20. Savings = x − 2x/5 − 3x/20 = 20x/20 − 8x/20 − 3x/20 = 9x/20. So 9x/20 = 5400 → x = 5400 × 20/9 = ₹12,000. Option C (₹15,000) comes from applying rent as 1/4 of the full salary instead of the remaining, giving savings = (1 − 2/5 − 1/4)x = 7x/20; 7x/20 = 5400 yields ≈ ₹15,429, which students round to ₹15,000. **Short Trick:** Savings fraction = (1 − 2/5) × (1 − 1/4) = 3/5 × 3/4 = 9/20. Salary = 5400 × 20/9 = 600 × 20 = ₹12,000.

questions.stem: What is the value of (3½ × 1⅓ + ¾) ÷ 2⅙?

options.option_text: The simplified result of the expression is 10/3
The simplified result of the expression is 5/2
The simplified result of the expression is 7/4
The simplified result of the expression is 9/4

questions.explanation: B is correct. Convert to improper fractions: 3½ = 7/2, 1⅓ = 4/3, ¾ = 3/4, 2⅙ = 13/6. Step 1 (multiply): 7/2 × 4/3 = 28/6 = 14/3. Step 2 (add ¾): 14/3 + 3/4 = 56/12 + 9/12 = 65/12. Step 3 (divide): 65/12 ÷ 13/6 = 65/12 × 6/13 = 5/2. Option C (7/4) results from skipping the ¾ term and dividing early: 14/3 ÷ 13/6 = 28/13 ≈ 2.15, then rounding. Option D (9/4) is a slip in the numerator sum in Step 2 (adding 9/12 + 4/12 instead of 9/12 + 8/12). **Short Trick:** In Step 3, cancel before multiplying — 65 and 13 share factor 13 (→ 5), and 6 and 12 share factor 6 (→ 2) — giving 5/2 instantly without full multiplication.

questions.stem: The decimal 0.363636... (where '36' repeats indefinitely) expressed as a fraction in its lowest terms is?

options.option_text: Expressed in its lowest terms, the recurring decimal equals 9/25
Expressed in its lowest terms, the recurring decimal equals 4/11
Expressed in its lowest terms, the recurring decimal equals 12/33
Expressed in its lowest terms, the recurring decimal equals 2/5

questions.explanation: B is correct. Let x = 0.363636... Since 2 digits repeat, multiply by 100: 100x = 36.3636... Subtracting: 99x = 36, so x = 36/99. Simplify: GCD(36, 99) = 9, giving 4/11. Option A (9/25 = 0.36 exactly) is wrong — 0.36 is a terminating decimal equal to 36/100, not 36/99. Option C (12/33) equals 4/11 but fails the 'lowest terms' requirement since GCD(12, 33) = 3. Option D (2/5 = 0.4) is an entirely different decimal. **Short Trick:** For a purely repeating decimal, place the repeating block over as many 9s as there are repeating digits. '36' has 2 digits → 36/99. Divide both by 9: 4/11. Done.

questions.stem: The numerator of a fraction is 4 less than its denominator. When 3 is added to both numerator and denominator, the fraction becomes 5/6. What is the original fraction?

options.option_text: The original fraction, before adding 3 to both parts, is 5/6
The original fraction, before adding 3 to both parts, is 17/21
The original fraction, before adding 3 to both parts, is 13/17
The original fraction, before adding 3 to both parts, is 14/18

questions.explanation: B is correct. Let denominator = d, numerator = d − 4. Adding 3 to both: (d − 1)/(d + 3) = 5/6. Cross-multiplying: 6d − 6 = 5d + 15 → d = 21, numerator = 17. Original fraction = 17/21. Verify: (17 + 3)/(21 + 3) = 20/24 = 5/6 ✓. Option A (5/6) is the fraction AFTER adding 3 — a classic misread of 'original'. Option C (13/17) satisfies the difference condition (17 − 13 = 4 ✓) but gives (16/20 = 4/5) ≠ 5/6 after adding 3. **Short Trick:** Adding the same number to both parts preserves the difference (denominator − numerator = 4). After adding 3, new fraction = 5/6; difference = 6k − 5k = k = 4, so 5k = 20, 6k = 24. Subtract 3 from each: numerator = 17, denominator = 21. Answer = 17/21 with no algebra.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper sold 3/8 of his stock on Monday, 2/5 of the remaining stock on Tuesday, and 1/6 of what was then left on Wednesday. If 270 kg of goods remained unsold after Wednesday, what was the original stock?

options.option_text: The total original stock of goods weighed 1,080 kg in all
The total original stock of goods weighed 864 kg in all
The total original stock of goods weighed 1,440 kg in all
The total original stock of goods weighed 1,296 kg in all

questions.explanation: B is correct. Unsold fraction after each day: After Monday: 1 − 3/8 = 5/8. After Tuesday: 5/8 × (1 − 2/5) = 5/8 × 3/5 = 3/8. After Wednesday: 3/8 × (1 − 1/6) = 3/8 × 5/6 = 5/16. So (5/16) × x = 270, giving x = 270 × 16/5 = 864 kg. Option A (1,080 kg): student uses 1/3 instead of 1/6 on Wednesday — remaining = 3/8 × 2/3 = x/4; x/4 = 270 → x = 1,080. Option C (1,440 kg): student applies Tuesday's 2/5 to the original stock, not to Monday's remainder — remaining after Tue = 5x/8 − 2x/5 = 9x/40; after Wed = 9x/40 × 5/6 = 3x/16; 3x/16 = 270 → x = 1,440. Option D (1,296 kg): student takes 1/6 of the original (not remaining) on Wednesday — left = 3x/8 − x/6 = 5x/24; 5x/24 = 270 → x = 1,296. **Short Trick:** Multiply the three 'unsold fractions' in one line: (5/8) × (3/5) × (5/6) = 75/240 = 5/16. Original = 270 × 16/5 = 54 × 16 = 864 kg.

questions.stem: If 0.6̄ denotes 0.6666..., 0.3̄ denotes 0.3333..., and 0.8̄ denotes 0.8888..., what is the value of (0.6̄ × 0.3̄ + 0.5) ÷ 0.8̄?

options.option_text: The final value after simplification is 17/20
The final value after simplification is 13/16
The final value after simplification is 52/81
The final value after simplification is 1/4

questions.explanation: B is correct. Convert: 0.6̄ = 6/9 = 2/3; 0.3̄ = 3/9 = 1/3; 0.8̄ = 8/9. Step 1: 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/9. Step 2: 2/9 + 1/2 = 4/18 + 9/18 = 13/18. Step 3: (13/18) ÷ (8/9) = 13/18 × 9/8 = 13/16. Option A (17/20 = 0.85) is the classic trap of treating all decimals as terminating: (0.6 × 0.3 + 0.5) ÷ 0.8 = 0.68/0.8 = 0.85. Option C (52/81) comes from inverting the wrong fraction in Step 3 — multiplying by 8/9 instead of 9/8: 13/18 × 8/9 = 104/162 = 52/81. Option D (1/4) results from omitting the +0.5 entirely: (2/9) ÷ (8/9) = 2/8 = 1/4. **Short Trick:** Single-digit repeaters convert instantly: 0.n̄ = n/9. So 0.6̄ = 2/3, 0.3̄ = 1/3, 0.8̄ = 8/9. In Step 3, cancel the 9 from 18 and 9 before multiplying: (13/18) × (9/8) = 13/(2 × 8) = 13/16.

questions.stem: How many fractions with denominator 15 lie strictly between 1/5 and 1/3?

options.option_text: Exactly 1 fraction — only 4/15 lies between 3/15 and 5/15
Exactly 2 fractions — both 4/15 and 2/15 qualify here
Exactly 3 fractions — 4/15, 6/15, and 7/15 all qualify
Exactly 0 fractions — no value with denominator 15 fits

questions.explanation: A is correct. Convert both bounds to denominator 15: 1/5 = 3/15 and 1/3 = 5/15. Fractions with denominator 15 strictly between 3/15 and 5/15 must have a numerator strictly between 3 and 5, i.e., only the integer 4. So exactly one fraction (4/15) qualifies. Option B is wrong because 2/15 < 1/5, placing it outside the range entirely. Option C is wrong because 6/15 = 2/5 > 1/3, also outside. Option D is wrong because 4/15 clearly satisfies 3/15 < 4/15 < 5/15. **Short Trick:** Convert bounds to the target denominator. Count integers strictly between the two resulting numerators: here between 3 and 5 → only 4. Answer = 1.

questions.stem: A recipe requires 2¾ cups of flour, 1½ cups of sugar, and ¾ cup of butter. What is the total quantity of all three ingredients combined?

options.option_text: 4½ cups total — adding all three ingredient amounts
5 cups total — sum of all three ingredient amounts
5¼ cups total — adding all three ingredient amounts
4¾ cups total — sum of all three ingredient amounts

questions.explanation: B is correct. Convert to improper fractions with denominator 4: 2¾ = 11/4, 1½ = 6/4, ¾ = 3/4. Sum = (11 + 6 + 3)/4 = 20/4 = 5 cups. Option A (4½) arises from incorrectly treating ¾ + ½ as 1 rather than 5/4. Option C (5¼) adds an extra ¼ due to a carry error. Option D (4¾) comes from wrongly summing 1½ + ¾ as 1¾ instead of 2¼. **Short Trick:** Split into whole and fractional parts. Whole: 2 + 1 + 0 = 3. Fractions: ¾ + ½ + ¾ = 3/4 + 2/4 + 3/4 = 8/4 = 2. Total = 3 + 2 = 5 cups.

questions.stem: A sum of money is divided among P, Q, and R in the ratio 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4. If R's share is ₹600, what is the total sum?

options.option_text: ₹2400 is the total sum distributed among P, Q, and R
₹2600 is the total sum distributed among P, Q, and R
₹3000 is the total sum distributed among P, Q, and R
₹2800 is the total sum distributed among P, Q, and R

questions.explanation: B is correct. Ratio 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4 — multiply every term by LCM(2,3,4) = 12 to get the integer ratio 6 : 4 : 3. Total parts = 13. R gets 3 parts = ₹600, so 1 part = ₹200. Total = 13 × 200 = ₹2600. Option A (₹2400) uses 12 total parts, forgetting to sum all three ratios correctly (6+4+3=13, not 12). Option C (₹3000) treats the share of R as 1/5 of the total. Option D (₹2800) uses 14 parts by miscounting. **Short Trick:** Fraction ratio → multiply by LCM of all denominators to clear fractions. R = 3 parts = ₹600 → unit = ₹200. Total = 13 units = ₹2600.

questions.stem: A fraction is first multiplied by 3/4 and then the result is divided by 7/5. The final value is 15/56. What is the original fraction?

options.option_text: 1/3 — one part out of three equal parts
1/2 — one part out of two equal parts
2/3 — two parts out of three equal parts
3/4 — three parts out of four equal parts

questions.explanation: B is correct. Let the fraction be F. Then F × (3/4) ÷ (7/5) = 15/56. Dividing by 7/5 is the same as multiplying by 5/7, giving F × (3/4) × (5/7) = F × 15/28 = 15/56. Therefore F = (15/56) × (28/15) = 28/56 = 1/2. Option A: 1/3 × 15/28 = 5/28 ≠ 15/56. Option C: 2/3 × 15/28 = 10/28 ≠ 15/56. Option D: 3/4 × 15/28 = 45/112 ≠ 15/56. **Short Trick:** Reverse the chain of operations — start from 15/56 and undo each step backwards. Undo ÷(7/5) by multiplying 15/56 × (7/5) = 105/280 = 3/8. Undo ×(3/4) by dividing 3/8 ÷ (3/4) = 3/8 × 4/3 = 12/24 = 1/2.

questions.stem: The recurring decimal 0.1233333... (where only the digit 3 repeats indefinitely after 0.12) expressed as a fraction in its lowest terms is?

options.option_text: 37/300, since 111/900 reduces by GCD 3 to give 37/300
11/90, applying the standard repeating-decimal fraction rule
41/333, treating 123 as the fully repeating block
37/270, derived from dividing 111 by 810 incorrectly

questions.explanation: A is correct. Let x = 0.12333.... Then 100x = 12.333... and 1000x = 123.333.... Subtracting: 900x = 111, giving x = 111/900. GCD(111, 900): 111 = 3 × 37; 900 = 3² × 4 × 25; GCD = 3. So x = 37/300. Verify: 37 ÷ 300 = 0.12333... ✓. Option B (11/90 = 0.1222...) arises from treating the digit 2 as the repeating part instead of 3. Option C (41/333) wrongly treats 123 as the repeating block, which would give 0.123123.... Option D has an arithmetic error in computing the denominator. **Short Trick:** For n non-repeating digits after the decimal point and m repeating digits, denominator = 10^(n+m) − 10^n and numerator = (full number ignoring decimal) − (non-repeating part). Here n=2, m=1: denominator = 1000 − 100 = 900; numerator = 123 − 12 = 111. Fraction = 111/900 = 37/300.

questions.stem: If x = 1 + 1 ÷ (1 + 1 ÷ (1 + 1/2)), what is the value of x?

options.option_text: 5/3, approximately equal to 1.667 as a decimal
8/5, exactly equal to 1.600 as a decimal
13/8, approximately equal to 1.625 as a decimal
3/2, exactly equal to 1.500 as a decimal

questions.explanation: B is correct. Evaluate strictly from the innermost bracket outward. Step 1 (innermost): 1 + 1/2 = 3/2. Step 2 (middle bracket): 1 + 1 ÷ (3/2) = 1 + 2/3 = 5/3. Step 3 (outermost): 1 + 1 ÷ (5/3) = 1 + 3/5 = 8/5. Option D (3/2) is only the innermost result — a student who stops too early gets this. Option A (5/3) is the middle-layer result, missing the final outer step. Option C (13/8) misapplies the Fibonacci-ratio pattern by adding neighbouring numerators and denominators: 5/3 → (5+8)/(3+5) = 13/8, which is incorrect here. **Short Trick:** In a continued fraction, work inside-out. The results form a Fibonacci sequence pattern: 3/2 → 5/3 → 8/5 (numerators 3,5,8 and denominators 2,3,5 are consecutive Fibonacci numbers). Each step: new = 1 + reciprocal(previous).

questions.stem: A proper fraction added to its own reciprocal gives 25/12. What is the sum of the numerator and denominator of that fraction?

options.option_text: The sum is 5, implying the fraction is 1/4 (p + q = 5)
The sum is 7, implying the fraction is 3/4 (p + q = 7)
The sum is 9, implying the fraction is 4/5 (p + q = 9)
The sum is 11, implying the fraction is 5/6 (p + q = 11)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Let the fraction be p/q with p < q (proper). Then p/q + q/p = 25/12, giving (p² + q²)/pq = 25/12, i.e., 12p² − 25pq + 12q² = 0. Dividing by q² and setting t = p/q: 12t² − 25t + 12 = 0. Discriminant = 625 − 576 = 49, so t = (25 ± 7)/24, yielding t = 32/24 = 4/3 or t = 18/24 = 3/4. Since p < q (proper fraction), t = 3/4, giving p = 3, q = 4, sum = 7. Verify: 3/4 + 4/3 = 9/12 + 16/12 = 25/12 ✓. Option A: 1/4 + 4/1 = 17/4 ≠ 25/12. Option C: 4/5 + 5/4 = 41/20 ≠ 25/12. Option D: 5/6 + 6/5 = 61/30 ≠ 25/12. **Short Trick:** Treat as x + 1/x = 25/12 → 12x² − 25x + 12 = 0. √discriminant = √49 = 7 (perfect square — a hallmark of a well-set exam problem). Roots = (25 ± 7)/24 = 4/3 or 3/4. Proper fraction → 3/4; sum of digits = 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.stem: If 5/7 of a number is equal to 4/9 of another number, what is the ratio of the first number to the second number?

options.option_text: 28 : 45 (correct: 5/7 × A = 4/9 × B gives A/B = 28/45)
45 : 28 (inverted ratio — gives second to first, not first to second)
20 : 63 (from computing 4×5 : 7×9 = 20:63, multiplying same-position terms)
36 : 35 (from computing 4×9 : 5×7 = 36:35, a cross-multiplication error)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Setting 5A/7 = 4B/9 and solving: A/B = (4/9) ÷ (5/7) = (4×7)/(9×5) = 28/45, giving the ratio A:B = 28:45. Option B (45:28) is the inverted ratio — a very common error where students lose track of which number is 'first'. Option C (20:63) arises from multiplying 4×5 and 7×9 directly (same positions) instead of cross-multiplying. **Short Trick:** When (a/b)×N₁ = (c/d)×N₂, ratio N₁:N₂ = (c×b):(d×a). Here: (4×7):(9×5) = 28:45. Simply cross-multiply the fractions and write as ratio — takes under 10 seconds.

questions.stem: What is the value of (3/4 ÷ 9/16) × (2/3 ÷ 4/9)?

options.option_text: 2 (the entire expression simplifies cleanly to a whole number)
3/2 (from computing only the second division 2/3 ÷ 4/9 = 3/2)
4/3 (from computing only the first division 3/4 ÷ 9/16 = 4/3)
32/81 (from not flipping the second divisor when dividing 2/3 by 4/9)

questions.explanation: A is correct. First bracket: 3/4 ÷ 9/16 = 3/4 × 16/9 = 48/36 = 4/3. Second bracket: 2/3 ÷ 4/9 = 2/3 × 9/4 = 18/12 = 3/2. Product: 4/3 × 3/2 = 12/6 = 2. Option D (32/81) is the classic error of forgetting to flip the divisor in the second bracket — computing 2/3 × 4/9 = 8/27 instead of 2/3 × 9/4 = 3/2, then multiplying 4/3 × 8/27 = 32/81. Options B and C are partial-computation traps. **Short Trick:** a/b ÷ c/d = (a×d)/(b×c). Combine both operations into one chain: (3×16)/(4×9) × (2×9)/(3×4). Cancel before multiplying: 16/4=4, 9/9=1, 3/3=1, 2/4=1/2 → the entire product = 4×(1/2) = 2.

questions.stem: If (x + 1/3) ÷ (x − 1/3) = 7/5, what is the value of x?

options.option_text: x = 6/5 (from misapplying componendo without the dividendo step)
x = 4 (from reading 2x = 4 as x = 4, skipping the final divide-by-2)
x = 1/2 (from treating 1/3 as a separate addend and dividing wrongly)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Cross-multiplying: 5(x + 1/3) = 7(x − 1/3) → 5x + 5/3 = 7x − 7/3 → 5/3 + 7/3 = 2x → 12/3 = 4 = 2x → x = 2. Verify: (2+1/3)/(2−1/3) = (7/3)/(5/3) = 7/5 ✓. Option C (x=4) is the critical error of stopping at 2x=4 and writing x=4 — forgetting to divide by 2. Option A (x=6/5) results from misapplying componendo alone. **Short Trick — Componendo-Dividendo:** If p/q = 7/5, then (p+q)/(p−q) = (7+5)/(7−5) = 12/2 = 6. Here p+q = 2x and p−q = 2/3. So 2x ÷ (2/3) = 6 → 3x = 6 → x = 2. This skips cross-multiplication entirely and saves two steps.

questions.stem: A water tank is 7/8 full. After drawing out some water it becomes 5/12 full. What fraction of the tank's total capacity was used?

options.option_text: 1/8 (from computing (7−5)/8 — subtracting numerators while keeping denominator)
2/3 (from treating 7/8 as 3/4 and computing 3/4 − 1/12 = 9/12 − 1/12)
5/12 (from approximating 7/8 as 3/4 and then computing 3/4 − 1/3 = 5/12)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Water used = 7/8 − 5/12. LCM(8, 12) = 24. Converting: 7/8 = 21/24 and 5/12 = 10/24. Difference = 11/24. Option A (1/8) is the most common beginner error — subtracting numerators directly (7−5=2) and writing 2/8=1/4 or 2/(8−0)=1/4... actually getting 1/8 by subtracting only numerators and misreading. Options C and D both stem from incorrectly rounding 7/8 to 3/4, then subtracting with different wrong values of 5/12. **Short Trick:** LCM(8,12): 8=2³, 12=2²×3, LCM=24. Scale 7/8 by ×3 → 21/24; scale 5/12 by ×2 → 10/24. Subtract: 11/24. Identify LCM by prime factorisation in one glance — no long division needed.

questions.stem: The decimal 0.1666... (where only the digit '6' repeats indefinitely, following a non-recurring '1') expressed as a fraction in its lowest terms is?

options.option_text: 16/99 (treating all digits as recurring — correct only for 0.1616... form)
1/6 (correct: mixed-recurring formula gives (16−1)/90 = 15/90 = 1/6)
8/45 (from using 16/90 without subtracting the non-recurring digit value)
2/11 (from misapplying the pure two-digit repeating block formula 16/88)

questions.explanation: B is correct. For a mixed recurring decimal 0.ab̄ (non-recurring digit a, then b repeating), the fraction = (full two-digit number − non-recurring part) / 90 = (16 − 1)/90 = 15/90 = 1/6. Verify: 1/6 = 0.16666... ✓. Option A (16/99) is the formula for a pure two-digit repeat — it equals 0.161616..., a different decimal. Option C (8/45 = 16/90) is the error of not subtracting the non-recurring digit. Option D (16/88) applies no standard rule correctly. **Short Trick — Mixed Recurring Formula:** 0.ab̄ → numerator = ab − a (remove non-recurring part), denominator = 90 (one 9 for each recurring digit, one 0 for each non-recurring digit before it). Two recurring digits? Denominator = 900. Always verify by dividing your fraction on paper.

questions.stem: What is the value of 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + 1/2))?

options.option_text: 3/2 (evaluated only the innermost bracket 1 + 1/2 and stopped there early)
5/3 (evaluated two levels deep but stopped before reaching the outermost +1)
8/5 (correct: inside-out evaluation — 3/2 → 5/3 → 8/5 at each level)
13/8 (from assuming one more nesting level exists beyond the expression)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Always evaluate from the innermost bracket outward. Step 1: 1 + 1/2 = 3/2. Step 2: 1 + 1/(3/2) = 1 + 2/3 = 5/3. Step 3: 1 + 1/(5/3) = 1 + 3/5 = 8/5. Options A and B are early-stopping errors at steps 1 and 2 respectively. Option D (13/8) is the next value in the sequence — a trap for students who miscount the depth of nesting. **Short Trick — Fibonacci Ratios:** The successive values in this family of nested fractions — 1/1, 2/1, 3/2, 5/3, 8/5, 13/8, 21/13 — follow the Fibonacci sequence. Each numerator = sum of previous two Fibonacci numbers. Here, starting from the innermost 1+1/2, three levels yield 3/2 → 5/3 → 8/5. Recognise the pattern and count levels: depth 3 gives the 5th Fibonacci ratio = 8/5.

questions.stem: A fraction becomes 1/3 when 1 is subtracted from its numerator and 1 is added to its denominator. It becomes 1/2 when 1 is added to both its numerator and denominator. What is the original fraction?

options.option_text: 3/7 (from misreading condition 1 as subtracting 1 from denominator instead of adding)
5/11 (the unique fraction satisfying both given conditions simultaneously)
3/5 (satisfies only condition 1: (3−1)/(5+1) = 1/3, but fails condition 2)
7/15 (satisfies only condition 2: (7+1)/(15+1) = 1/2, but fails condition 1)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Let the fraction be p/q. Condition 1: (p−1)/(q+1) = 1/3 → 3p − q = 4 ...(i). Condition 2: (p+1)/(q+1) = 1/2 → 2p − q = −1 ...(ii). Subtract (ii) from (i): p = 5. Substitute into (ii): 10 − q = −1 → q = 11. Original fraction = 5/11. Verify: (5−1)/(11+1) = 4/12 = 1/3 ✓; (5+1)/(11+1) = 6/12 = 1/2 ✓. Option A (3/7) is the answer obtained if condition 1 is misread as subtracting 1 from the denominator — solving (p−1)/(q−1)=1/3 and (p+1)/(q+1)=1/2 gives p=3, q=7. Options C and D each satisfy exactly one condition, expertly designed to trap students who verify only one constraint. **Short Trick:** Always set up both equations and eliminate q by direct subtraction. Single-equation trial-and-error will produce multiple candidates (C, D) — only the system of two equations pins the unique answer.
